newsitem.title: USA: Jury can consider Florida role as cigarette maker -judge.
newsitem.headline: Jury can consider Florida role as cigarette maker -judge.

text.p: Florida's role as a cigarette maker and distributor can be considered in assessing damages if a Florida jury finds the tobacco companies guilty of racketeering and fraud, a judge ruled Tuesday.
Jury selection is scheduled to begin Friday in Florida's lawsuit seeking to recover Medicaid costs for treating tobacco-related illness.

The state has sought to prevent the jury from learning that Florida made cigarettes in state prisons from 1935 through 1978, when it went out of the business. The cigarettes were made by prisoners and were distributed to inmates and sold in state hospitals, health facilities and other state and county offices.

But Palm Beach County Circuit Judge Harold Cohen ruled Tuesday that the jury could consider the state's action in assessing penalties against the tobacco companies if the panel finds the cigarette makers guilty of defruading the public about the health danger of smoking.
The question arose as Cohen was attempting to determine what evidence the jury ultimately will be allowed to hear when the case goes to trial.
Earlier Tuesday, Cohen refused to dismiss the state's racketeering and fraudulent advertising charges against the tobacco industry.

Cohen said the evidence did not show that Florida had knowingly encouraged tobacco companies to use false information or to manufacture false science in order to protect its own interest in selling cigarettes.

Robert Blakey, a Notre Dame University law professor and expert on U.S. and Florida racketeering statutes, told Cohen that if the state misled the tobacco companies about what they could sell in Florida, the racketeering and false advertising charges should be dismissed.
While the state "did some bad things, it is not the kind of due process offence" that would merit dismissal of the fraud and racketeering counts, Cohen ruled.
He left open the possibility of revisiting the issue if the tobacco companies were able to present more compelling evidence in the future.
Tobacco manufacturers presented Cohen with documents that indicated the the state knew that its own Board of Health in 1906 considered cigarettes the "worst form of addiction."
As early as the 1960s, state health officials had linked cigarette smoking to heart disease, lung cancer and emphysema, the tobacco companies showed with the documents.

Stephen Krigbaum, an attorney for Philip Morris Cos. Inc., told Cohen that Florida continued to promote the tobacco industry and that even today it markets Florida-grown tobacco for use in other countries.
Krigbaum argued the state broke its own laws by providing cigarettes to minors. He added that when the tobacco industry launched a stop-smoking programme aimed at minors, Florida called it off.
